verdict: UHS revenue rose 5% to $4.7B across its hospitals and behavioral-health centers, but bigger liability reserves and higher interest costs cut profit attributable to UHS to $309M from $373M a year ago.

kpis.label: Revenue growth
kpis.note: net revenues $4.7B vs $4.5B a year ago

kpis.label: EPS (GAAP)
kpis.note: diluted, attributable to UHS, vs $5.86 a year ago

kpis.label: Acute Care revenue
kpis.note: up 5% YoY — general hospitals were 58% of revenue

kpis.label: Adjusted EBITDA
kpis.note: adjusted EBITDA net of noncontrolling interests (non-GAAP), vs $671M a year ago

segments.name: Acute Care
segments.note: General and surgical hospitals — emergency care, surgery and inpatient treatment. Revenue rose 5% on more admissions; revenue per adjusted admission fell slightly at long-held hospitals.

segments.name: Behavioral Health
segments.note: Psychiatric and addiction-treatment facilities — UHS's other big business, and usually its steadier earner. Revenue rose 6%.

segments.name: Other
segments.note: Corporate and other revenue, net of eliminations between the two hospital businesses — a small residual line so the segments tie to the $4,733M consolidated total.

opex.name: Depreciation & amortization
opex.note: Spreading the cost of hospitals, buildings and equipment over their working lives.

otherDetail: Net interest expense of $56M, partly offset by $16M of other income — a net $40M cost below operating income. Total net income was $313M; $5M of it went to noncontrolling interests, leaving $309M attributable to UHS.
follow100Note: The cost rows above break down the $4,104M cost of revenue and the depreciation line: salaries, wages and benefits of $2,210M are the direct cost of care, alongside $1,426M of other operating expenses, $427M of supplies and $41M of lease and rental expense — the statement's operating-charge lines, grouped the same way as the flow.

takeaways.title: Both hospital businesses grew
takeaways.text: Net revenues rose 5.3% to $4,733M. Acute Care revenue rose 5% to $2,764M and Behavioral Health rose 6% to $1,966M, on more admissions in both businesses.

takeaways.title: Liability reserves took a bite
takeaways.text: UHS added $26M to its reserves for self-insured professional and general liability claims — tied to a tentative settlement — and interest expense rose to $56M from $38M. Income from operations fell to $454M from $522M despite the revenue growth.

takeaways.title: Medicaid payments helped
takeaways.text: Increases in Medicaid supplemental payments (extra state payments for treating Medicaid patients, mainly in Washington, D.C. and California) added a favorable $47M before tax, net of related provider taxes — partly offsetting the $26M reserve increase, for a net favorable $21M that was not in UHS's forecast.

oneTimers: Two items UHS says were not in its forecast netted to a favorable $21M before tax: a $47M favorable impact from higher Medicaid supplemental payments (net of provider taxes), partly offset by a $26M increase in self-insured liability reserves tied to a tentative legal settlement.
footerNote: Hospitals report no gross-profit line: cost of revenue here groups the direct cost of care — salaries and benefits, other operating expenses, supplies, and lease and rental expense — with depreciation and amortization as the operating expense below it, following the statement's operating-charge lines. The flow ties to consolidated net income of $313M, before the $5M attributable to noncontrolling interests.
